Evaluating the effectiveness of alkylammonium halide-based deep eutectic solvent pretreatments in heightening carbohydrates and lignin separation from poplar sawdust
Wei Tang a,¹, Ruolin Li b,¹, Xinyue Wang a, Haojie Qian a, Bo Fan a, Yucai He a,*

a School of Pharmacy & School of Biological and Food Engineering, Changzhou University, Changzhou 213164, Jiangsu Province, China b Jiangsu Co-Innovation Center of Efficient Processing and Utilization of Forest Resources, College of Chemical Engineering, Nanjing Forestry University, Nanjing 210037, China
## ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Deep eutectic solvent pretreatment poplar sawdust cetyltrimethylammonium bromide

ABSTRACT The molecular architecture of hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA) within deep eutectic solvents (DES) emerges as a key factor in bioconversion of lignocellulose. This work constructed a series of DES systems by employing diverse alkylammonium halide as HBAs, enabling an investigation into the synergistic interplay between alkyl chain length and halide anion identity on the deconstruction of poplar sawdust (PS). Notably, the cetyl-trimethylammonium bromide (CTAB)-based DES displayed a reduced surface potential, weakened hydrogen bonding energy, and diminished polarity, outperforming counterparts based on short-chain alkylamines or alternative halide-containing HBA. When applied in the pretreatment of PS, this DES has achieved a removal of 68.4% lignin and 94.0% xylan, while elevating the cellulose digestibility to 76.5%. Structural analysis unveiled that the CTAB-based DES profoundly disrupted the pivotal β-O-4 ether bonds and aromatic structure within lignin, and thus enhancing substrate digestibility. The long-chain hydrophobic alkyl chains and highly-polar bromide ions empowered the DES with superior penetration and deconstruction capabilities toward lignocellulose, highlighting the paramount significance of HBA's molecular structure in refining DES pretreatment paradigms for efficient biomass transformation.

# 1. Introduction The overreliance on fossil resources and the challenges posed by global climate change necessitates the emergence of renewable re- sources as a solution to the energy crisis [1]. The bioconversion of abundant and renewable lignocellulosic biomass into green bioenergy is anticipated to facilitate the sustainable development of industrialization [2,3]. Populus euramericana, a species extensively cultivated across temperate and cold-temperate zones of the Northern Hemisphere, is prized for its remarkable adaptability and pivotal role in industrial timber production [4]. However, during the processes of harvesting and manufacturing, approximately 30 % of the resulting byproduct mani- fests as fine particulate matter, commonly known as poplar sawdust (PS) [5]. Much like other lignocellulosic biomass, PS predominantly consists of glucan and xylan, which constitute the fundamental framework of its carbohydrate-rich structure [6]. As such, transforming PS into bioenergy
not only presents a promising economic opportunity but also embodies a sustainable and ecologically responsible strategy for waste valorization.

It is widely recognized that lignin, which envelops bioglycans such as cellulose and hemicellulose, forms a complex barrier structure that significantly impedes the biotransformation of lignocellulose [7]. To achieve efficient conversion of wood-based lignocellulose, selecting appropriate delignification pretreatment methods is crucial [8]. Nevertheless, traditional delignification pretreatments always have inherent drawbacks that have limited the development of biorefineries [9]. For instance, the oxidative methods frequently resulted in severe cellulose degradation through over-oxidation [1]. Alkaline processes gave rise to copious amounts of saline effluent [10]. Organic solvent- based systems incurred prohibitively high operational expenses, while ionic liquid treatments were plagued by excessive viscosity and inade- quate process efficiency [11]. Oppositely, deep eutectic solvents (DES), which are green and biocompatible mixtures formed by hydrogen bond

donors (HBD) and acceptors (HBA), have emerged as preferred reaction media for pretreatment [11,12]. The hydrogen bonds between HBA and HBD are the predominant internal non-covalent interactions, playing a crucial role in disrupting the lignocellulosic barrier structure [13]. During the DES pretreatment, the most widely recognized delignifica- tion mechanism involved the protons generated from the dissociation of HBD catalyzing the cleavage of ether or ester bonds between lignin and polysaccharide components [14,15]. Furthermore, the HBA would also cleave the Cα site of lignin, subsequently facilitating the cleavage of the β-O-4 bond and generating Hibbert's ketones [16]. For various DES, key properties influencing lignin dissolution included viscosity, pKa, hydrogen bond basicity, and Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters, all closely related to HBA characteristics [17]. Therefore, while numerous studies have concentrated on the relationship between HBD of DES and pretreatment performance, it was undeniable that HBAs also played a crucial role in determining the solubility of lignin in DES [15].

According to the existing literature, DES prepared using HBD pri- marily comprised organic acids and polyols, whereas HBA predomi- nantly consisted of choline chloride (ChCl) and betaine [14,18]. Regarding pretreatment performance, organic acid-based DES enriched with -COOH and -OH groups exhibited strong correlations with delignification efficiency [19,20]. This was attributed to these organic acids significantly enhancing hemicellulose removal by catalyzing the disintegration of glycosidic bonds and acetyl groups, thereby intensi- fying the degradation of lignin [5]. For instance, Tian et al. found that formic acid, acetic acid, and lactic acid-based DES achieved delignifi- cation extents of 73–77 % and selectivity up to 6 % when treating PS [21]. Hou et al. discovered that the strong electron-withdrawing groups and low pKa of the HBD in acid-based DES facilitated the dissolution of xylan from rice straw [22]. To achieve higher efficiency, acid-based DES can be combined with acid auxiliary agents, such as inorganic acids or metal chlorides, to form ternary DES, thereby ulteriorly improving the depolymerization of xylan and lignin [23,24]. Numerous studies have focused on enhancing the performance of acid-based DES pretreatment by optimizing the acidity or diversity of HBD, while overlooking the potential of alternative HBA beyond quaternary ammonium salts. Ling et al. treated bamboo with DES prepared from different HBA, specif- ically acetamide, betaine, and ChCl. They discovered that levulinic acid/ ChCl exhibited the strongest delignification properties, while levulinic acid/betaine demonstrated superior lignin recovery capabilities [25]. Additionally, it has been reported that a shorter-alkyl-chain in quater- nary ammonium salts within DES was more favorable for the dissolution of lignin and xylan, indicating that the selectivity of the HBA signifi- cantly influenced pretreatment performance [19]. Our previously works also found that DES prepared by alkylammonium bromide/chloride has unpredictable effects during pretreatments [26]. Specifically, the syn- ergistic effect of cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) combined with lactic acid (LA) could achieve the removal of more than 50 % of lignin and 73 % of xylan [27]. This violently disrupted the natural structure of lignocellulose, thereby validating the potential of alky- lammonium halide-based DES in biorefinery applications. As the HBA of DES, alkylammonium halides not only exhibited electron-dense domains adept at forming robust hydrogen bonds that promoted efficient eutectic formation, but also boasted extended hydrocarbon chains that conferred pronounced hydrophobicity upon the solvent matrix [28]. This inherent lipophilic character may potentially enhance the extraction efficacy of hydrophobic constituents from lignocellulose. Despite these promising attributes, previous researches have largely been limited to preliminary evaluations of DES pretreatment performance. A deeper mechanistic understanding of how critical structural parameters of HBA (such as the alkyl chain length, the halogen atom type, and the functional group architecture of alkylammonium halides) influenced the overall effi- ciency of the pretreatment process remained strikingly underexplored. Moreover, the relationship between the structural features of DES’s HBA and the deconstruction of lignin required further elucidation. The objective of this study was to investigate the competitive behavior of

alkylammonium or ChCl-based DES in the separation of PS components, and to evaluate the potential applications of lower-cost and higher- biocompatibility alkylammonium halides in biorefining processes.

In this study, DES were prepared by combining three types of alkylammonium salts or ChCl with LA. The structural characteristics of the prepared DES were thoroughly analyzed using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), proton nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and Quantum theoretical calculation. Subsequently, these DES were utilized for PS pretreatment, and the cellulose digestibility of the pretreated PS was evaluated. The effects of DES on PS were examined through changes in crystal structure, accessibility, lignin surface area, and lignin structural characterization. Finally, the recyclability of the DES was examined to evaluate their potential application in lignocellulosic pretreatment, and recommendations for optimizing DES pretreatment were provided.

2. Materials and methods 2.1. Materials The PS was sourced from the Huayuan Wood Processing Plant nestled in Jiangsu Province, China. CTAB, dodecyl trimethylammonium Bromide (DTAB), hexadecyl trimethylammonium chloride (CTAC), and ChCl were procured from Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. LA and other chemical reagents were obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Group based in Shanghai, China. The commercial cellulase (Cellic CTec2.0) with a filter paper enzyme activity measured at 205 FPU/g was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich's Shanghai branch.

2.2. *Preparation and characterization of DES* Various HBA (ChCl, CTAB, DTAB, and CTAC) was mixed with HBD (LA) in 500-mL round-bottomed flasks at molar ratios of 1:2, 1:4, 1:6, and 1:8. The flasks were subsequently sealed and stirred at a constant temperature of 80 °C until transparent and homogeneous solutions were formed. The resulting DES were designated as CCL, CBL, DBL, and CAL, corresponding to the respective HBA used (ChCl, CTAB, DTAB, and CTAC).

The functional groups of DES were investigated at ambient temper- atura using FTIR spectrometers (Shimadzu, Japan). The instrument was operated at 40 kV and 15 mA, and the FTIR spectra were recorded in the wavenumber range of 4000–500 cm⁻¹. The thermostability of DES was evaluated by TGA using a Rigaku TGA 8122 instrument (Japan) under a nitrogen atmosphere. The TGA measurements were conducted at a constant heating rate of 10 °C/min over a temperature range of 50 °C to 550 °C. Additionally, the proton signals of DES dissolved in DMSO-d₆ were analyzed by ¹H NMR spectroscopy using a 400 MHz Bruker AVANCE instrument. The Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters were deter- mined based on previous literature using N, N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline, 4- nitroaniline, and Nile red as probes.

2.3. Pretreatment and enzymatic hydrolysis of PS The PS with a dry weight of 20 g was suspended in diverse DES solutions at a mass ratio of 1:20. The round-bottomed flask containing the mixture was subsequently immersed in an oil bath and stirred at a temperature of 80–140 °C for 60 min. Following this, the pretreated PS and the DES was separated and recovered via vacuum filtration. The pretreated PS was then extensively cycled-washed with hot distilled water (60 °C) to remove the residual DES solvents [29]. After washing, the PS was stored at 4 °C for future use, while the recovered DES was reused for subsequent PS pretreatment according to the aforementioned procedure.

## 2.6. Isolation and characterization of lignin The isolation of milled wood lignin (Björkman lignin) from raw and DES-pretreated PS was conducted for Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) analysis. Initially, 10 g of samples were subjected to ball milling for 48 h at 360 rpm using a planetary ball mill (JX-4G, Jingxin Indus- trial, China). The resulting powders were subsequently dispersed in a 96 % aqueous dioxane solution and stirred at 150 rpm for 24 h with this process repeated three times. The suspension was then centrifuged at 5000 g for 5 min to isolate the lignin extract. The isolated extract was rotary evaporated to yield a coarse lignin powder. Lignin purification was conducted sequentially using a 10 wt% dichloroethane/ethanol mixture (2:1, v/v), followed by ether treatment and air drying. The milled wood lignin in PS derived from CCL, CBL, DBL, and CAL pre- treated PS were designated as LCCL, LCBL, LDBL, and LCAL, respectively. ## 2.7. Quantum theory analysis of DES and DES:VG The molecular structures of CTAB, CTAC, DTAB, ChCl and LA were optimized by Gaussian09 at M062X/6-311 + g(d,p) level [17]. The lignin model compound utilized in this study was veratrylglycerol-β-guaiacyl ether (VG), which contained β-O-4 ether linkages, aromatic hydroxyl groups, and two aliphatic hydroxyl groups. The cluster structures of various DES and their clusters formed with VG were constructed using MOPAC and Gaussian09 programs. For each cluster, 20 random cluster configurations were generated. These configurations were initially optimized semi-empirically at the PM6-DH⁺ level, followed by further refinement using Gaussian09 at the B3LYP/6-31G* level to obtain detailed molecular electrostatic potential information. The electron density (ρBCP) and the Laplace of the electron density (∇²ρBCP) were calculated for each DES and their clusters formed with VG. Ultimately, the lowest-energy configuration was selected from the 20 random configurations, and subsequent analyses were performed using the Multiwfn program, including molecular surface electrostatic potential calculations, atoms-in-molecules (AIM) analysis, and Independent Gradient Model with Hydrogen (IGMH) analysis.

## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Property difference of DES #### 3.1.1. Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters To investigate the unique properties of DES, four distinct samples composed of ChCl:LA (CCL), CTAB:LA (CBL), DTAB:LA (DBL), and CTAC:LA (CAL) were prepared with a molar ratio of HBD to HBA set at 1:4. The multiparametric K-T parameters including the hydrogen bond acidity (α), hydrogen bond basicity (β), and polarizability (π*), were utilized to quantitatively evaluate the polarity characteristics of these DES [30]. As presented in Table 1, alkylammonium-based DES have the lower π* values compared to traditional CCL, specifically 0.83 for CBL, 0.59 for DBL, and 0.31 for CAL. Given that HBD was consistently comprised of an equal amount of LA, the predominant factors influencing the polarizability of these DES were attributed to the structural characteristics of HBA [31,32]. Specifically, the O in -OH group of the ChCl molecule possessed high electronegativity, whereas the C in -CH3 group of the alkylammonium-based DES displayed relatively uniform electronegativity [33]. Additionally, due to the lower electronegativity of Br⁻ compared to Cl⁻, the positive charge distribution in the CTAB molecule was more concentrated, resulting in higher polarity [34]. Notably, the DTAB with shorter alkyl chain had higher polarity than CTAB, likely due to differences in solubility and amphiphilicity [35]. Table 1 also presented the β parameter, which quantified the ability of DES to facilitate proton association through hydrogen bonding. The values were ranked as follows: CAL (1.08) > DBL (1.02) > CCL (0.74) > CBL (0.57). The capability of HBA to form hydrogen bonds was primarily characterized by its ability to donate electron density [36]. Specifically, the N in quaternary ammonium structures of both ChCl or alkylammonium halides could provide electron density, thereby facilitating hydrogen bond formation [37,38]. However, CTAB with longer alkyl chain allows C to contribute indistinctively to electron density

Furthermore, the ammonium bromide exhibited greater flexibility compared to the ammonium chloride due to the smaller size of Br relative to Cl, leading to a stronger electron density for CTAC than CTAB [39]. Upon the formation of hydrogen bonds between HBA and protons from HBD, the electron density of DES became moderated, correlating closely with the β value of DES [40]. The parameter α was frequently employed to quantify the acidity of DES or its proton-donating capa- bility [19]. As shown in Table 1, the α of CCL, CBL, DBL, and CAL were 1.38, 1.27, 1.32, and 1.17, respectively. Even with the identical HBD, DES displayed varying proton-supplying capacities, which were also closely related to the characteristics of HBA. Studies have shown that ChCl exhibited greater instability under acidic conditions compared to CTAB, negatively impacting its proton-providing capability associated with HBD [40]. Conversely, CTAB, with longer alkyl chain and acid instability, demonstrated adverse proton acceptance performance [41]. Moreover, CTAB was less likely to provide protons compared to CTAC due to the higher stability of Br⁻ relative to Cl⁻ [35]. In summary, the K- T parameter characteristics of DES showed a profound and intricate relationship with the structural attributes of HBA, consequently influ- encing the dissolution behavior of non-polar polymers. Among the four DES, the CBL with CTAB as HBA possessed the lowest β and highest α value, despite its π* being marginally lower than that of CCL.

### 3.1.2. Changes in structural features The FTIR spectra of DES labeled with key functional groups were presented in Fig. 1a. The characteristic peak at 3445 cm⁻¹ was attributed to the stretching vibration of -OH in CCL or -NH₃⁺ in CBL, DEL, or CAL [42]. The broad peaks and significant vibration amplitude observed for CBL suggested the formation of hydrogen bonds between N and H within the CBL structure. The peaks at 2924 cm⁻¹ and 2852 cm⁻¹ corresponded to the characteristic stretching vibration of -CH₃ and -CH₂ in alkylammonium-based DES [21]. The peak at 1742 cm⁻¹ was assigned to the C=O stretching vibration in LA, with its reduced intensity indicating weakened hydrogen bonding interactions due to HBD [5]. The C-N stretching vibrations were observed at 1637 cm⁻¹ and 1127 cm⁻¹. The prominent peak areas of CBL and CAL may be attributed to the presence of internal covalent bonding within alkylammonium structure [43]. The peaks at 1473 cm⁻¹ and 1403 cm⁻¹ were attributed to in-plane and out-of-plane scissoring vibrations of the -CH₃ or -CH₂ in HBA, respectively. Notably, the out-of-plane scissoring peak intensity for -CH₃ and -CH₂ in CBL was significantly higher, which may be due to increased internal forces leading to enhanced vibrational amplitude [25]. The peaks at 1232 cm⁻¹ and 949 cm⁻¹ correspond to the stretching vibrations of C-O. The prominence of the C-O stretching vibration in DBL suggested that the O in this DES actively participated in hydrogen bond formation [44]. Based on the FTIR spectra analysis, it was reasonable to deduce that the N and O in the four DES likely serve as pivotal contributors to the establishment of enhanced hydrogen bonding networks. The ¹H NMR spectrum was used to further validate and refine the structure information of various DES. As illustrated in Fig. 1b, the peaks observed at 3.4 ppm was likely attributable to the proton signal arising from the internal hydrogen bond within the DES. The peaks around 4.8 ppm corresponded to the proton signals of the methine group in LA [15]. The peaks at 3.1 ppm, 2.5 ppm, 1.3 ppm, and 0.9 ppm were attributed to the methylene group bonded to the halogen element, the methyl group attached to the amino group, and the methylene group on the alkyl chain, respectively [32]. The peak at 4.1 ppm was attributed to the characteristic signal of hydrogen in the -COOH [45]. The appearance of proton peak associated with hydrogen bond indicated that alkylammonium halides were a viable strategy for preparing DES. Notably, the hydrogen bond peaks observed for DBL and CCL were more pronounced, potentially indicating stronger hydrogen bond interactions. Furthermore, TGA was employed to assess the thermostability of DES. As shown in Fig. 1c and d, CBL demonstrated superior thermal stability, with a mass loss of less than 10 % when heated to 186 °C. 3.1.3. Quantum chemical calculation Atoms in Molecules (AIM) theory was employed to investigate the intermolecular interactions within the DES [17]. Fig. 2a illustrated the bond critical points (BCP) associated with hydrogen bonds in the four DES, while Table S1 summarized the corresponding electron density (ρBCP) and Laplace function of the electron density (∇²ρBCP). According to AIM theory, the standard range of ρBCP in hydrogen bonds was 0.002 to 0.035 a.u., and the ∇²ρBCP values generally fell between 0.024 and 0.139 a.u. [15,44]. The ρBCP and ∇²ρBCP values between HBA and HBD for all four DES were within these specified ranges, confirming that their predominant interaction mode was hydrogen bonding. Subsequently, the hydrogen bond energy (HBE) was calculated and categorized into four classes: weak (> − 2.5 kcal/mol), weak-medium (−2.5 to −14.0 kcal/mol), medium (−15.0 to −11.0 kcal/mol), and strong (<−15.0 kcal/mol) [44]. According to Table S1, the HBE between the halogen ions of CTAB, CTAC and DTAB with LA were − 7.656, −8.681 and − 9.848 kcal/mol, respectively. In contrast, the HBE between Cl in ChCl and LA was measured at −8.829 kcal/mol. These findings suggested that alkylammonium halide-based DES exhibited strong internal hydrogen bonding, with the most pronounced effect observed in short-chain brominated DTAB as HBA. Fig. 2b presented a van der Waals surface diagram illustrating the electrostatic potential coloring for various DES. Notably, there were negative electrostatic potentials near the Cl⁻ or Br⁻ of the HBA and the hydroxyl O of LA, while substantial positive potentials were observed near H and methyl groups. This confirmed that the pronounced negative potential surrounding functional group indicated their suitability as HBA, whereas the strong positive potential suggested their appropriateness as HBD [48]. The formation of hydrogen bonds between the HBD and HBA led to charge delocalization, thereby facilitating the formation of DES [49]. The electrostatic potential values of CCL, CBL, DBL, and CAL ranged from −39.58 to 66.95 kJ/mol, −48.67 to 44.23 kJ/mol, −53.31 to 46.18 kJ/mol, and − 57.07 to 46.80 kJ/mol, respectively. It was evident that the negative potential in CAL was more pronounced compared to the other

DES, indicating a stronger interaction force between CTAC and LA within CAL. Additionally, the positive potential of CCL was more pronounced compared to the other three DES, likely due to multiple hydrogen bonds formed between the alkyl chains of the long-chain HBA and LA, as well as complementarity interactions between positive and negative regions [39]. These factors significantly diminished the energy and reduced the positive potential surrounding the valence group [47]. Fig. 3a illustrated the quantitative distribution of electrostatic potential for various DES, which aligned with the van der Waals surface diagrams. It was observed that DBL and CAL exhibited extensive charged regions, followed by CBL and CCL. This suggested that DTAB and CTAC have stronger interactions with DES formed by LA. Fig. 4a-4d presented the IGMH plots for various DES, serving as a computational method to visualize weak interactions. Within the isosurface formed between HBA and HBD, it was evident that the primary weak interactions occurred between the -OH in HBD and the Cl$^{-}$ or Br$^{-}$ of HBA. In the IGMH scatter plot of CCL, the density of blue scatter points was notably higher than that of green scatter points, indicating that hydrogen bonding was the predominant interaction between ChCl and LA. In the IGMH scatter plots of the other DES, the density in the green area was significantly greater, suggesting a strong van der Waals forces in CBL, DBL, and CAL. Furthermore, the blue region in DBL showed a higher density compared to that in CAL, with CBL exhibiting the lowest density. This observation also indicated that the DES prepared from the short-chain and brominated DTAB as well as CCL, demonstrated stronger hydrogen bonding, whereas the hydrogen bonding between the long-chain CTAB and LA was considerably weaker.

It has mentioned that the DES prepared with short-chain DTAB or chlorinated CTAC possessed higher hydrogen bond associations than CBL, but the depolymerization of lignin during pretreatment was inferior to that observed with CBL pretreatment. Hou et al. discovered that the hydrogen bond strength in DES was inversely proportional to their pretreatment efficiency, and the DES with higher hydrogen bond energy exhibited reduced lignin depolymerization [22]. Hence, as the hydrogen bond energy of DES decreased in the following order of CAL > DBL > CCL > CBL, the depolymerization and removal efficiency of lignin progressively increased in this work.

3.5.2. Quantum chemical calculation between DES and lignin model The formation of a stable structure between DES and lignin is crucial for effective lignin dissolution during DES pretreatment. Therefore, the veratrylglycerol-β-guaiacyl ether (VG) was selected as a lignin model compound for quantum chemical calculations involving four DES systems [58]. Fig. 2a and b displayed the AIM molecular graphs and van der Waals surface maps with electrostatic potential coloring for four DES:VG clusters. In all clusters, the minimum electrostatic potential occurred near Cl⁻ or Br⁻, with values of −47.55 kcal/mol (CCL-VG), −47.34 kcal/mol (DBL-VG), −46.06 kcal/mol (CAL-VG), and − 43.72 kcal/mol (CBL-VG). The lower absolute value of the electrostatic potential suggested weaker HBD-HBA interactions, which facilitated the formation of a hydrogen bond network between DES and VG. This stabilization enhanced the structural integrity of VG and improved lignin removal. Fig. 3b illustrated the quantitative distribution of electrostatic potential for four DES:VG clusters, aligning with the van der Waals surface diagram depicting electrostatic potential filling. It was evident that CBL:VG cluster exhibited a substantial area near an electrostatic potential of

zero, followed by CAL:VG and DBL:VG, while CCL:VG displayed a notably smaller charged area. This suggested that CBL has wider inter- action areas and stronger internal interactions with VG, consistent with its superior delignification performance. Subsequently, the intermolec- ular interactions were investigated using AIM theory. Fig. 3b showed the BCP representing the hydrogen bonds between the four DES:VG, while Table S1 summarized the pBCP and V²pBCP. As shown in Fig. 3b and Table S1, the interaction sites in CCL:VG were relatively straightfor- ward, primarily involving the alcohol hydroxyl group of VG. The pBCP of the bond between the O of -OH and CCL was 0.0411, with a bond energy of -8.4564 kcal/mol, which fell within the covalent bond cate- gory. However, the molecular size of ChCl was considerably smaller than that of lignin, thereby restricting the effective interaction surface area and potential interactions between them. DBL established hydrogen bonds with both the ether bond and -OH of VG. Notably, the strongest interaction was observed between DTAB and the O of -OH in VG, characterized by a pBCP value of 0.0222 and a bond energy of -4.2308 kcal/mol. In contrast, CAL formed relatively weak hydrogen bonds with both the ether bond and -OH of VG. Most prominently, CBL primarily interacted with the ether bond, alcohol hydroxyl group, and phenolic hydroxyl group of VG, resulting in the formation of multiple bond crit- ical points. Notably, the strongest interaction was observed between LA and the O of the alcohol hydroxyl group of VG, characterized by a pBCP value of 0.0510 and a bond energy of -10.6605 kcal/mol, which belonged to the covalent bond category [44]. This further suggested that CBL exhibited a more stable covalent bond structure with lignin compared to CCL, thereby accelerating the dissolution process of lignin. Fig. 4e-4h was the IGMH diagram, a computational method for visual- izing weak interactions. The IGMH diagram corroborated the findings from the electrostatic potential surface diagram and AIM diagram. Specifically, the IGMH scatter plot of CBL:VG has a greater number and density of scatter points than the other three, with an additional peak of blue scatter points indicative of hydrogen bonding interactions. It could be inferred that the CBL:VG has stronger van der Waals force and hydrogen bonding interaction. The formation of stronger hydrogen bonds theoretically indicated that lignin rich in β-O-4 was more easily dissolved in CBL, and the quantitative results of lignin linkage bonds well confirmed this.

In conclusion, DES effectively broke the β-O-4 ether bonds and C—C bonds in lignin through the hydrogen bond system formed between alkylammonium and LA. Electrostatic potential mapping unveiled that the CBL and VG aggregates preferentially localize within regions of zero electric potential, suggesting an inverse relationship between hydrogen bond intensity and lignin's depolymerization efficacy. AIM further confirmed that strong covalent interactions formed between the -OH of CBL and VG, with a bond energy of –10.6605 kcal/mol, significantly higher than other types of DES, underscoring that the hydrogen bond network between CBL and lignin helped to effectively remove lignin. ³¹P NMR analysis unveiled a marked decline in aliphatic OH content from 7.46 mmol/g to 4.11 mmol/g after CBL pretreatment, while the contents of phenolic OH and carboxyl groups exhibited a conspicuous rise. This intricate transformation paved the way for the establishment of new covalent linkages between DES and lignin, directly resulting in a reduction in the content of β-O-4 linkages from 58.4/100 Ar to 39.8/100 Ar. 2D-HSQC analysis further revealed that the G units were more vulnerable to oxidative degradation compared to S units in the Lʀ. The S/G ratio increased from 1.0 to 1.4 after CBL pretreatment, marking the most dramatic shift among all pretreatments. This increase was pri- marily driven by protons donated by DES, which actively catalyzed the cleavage of methoxy groups from lignin's aromatic framework. Notably, the negative correlation between hydrogen bond strength and the demethoxylation extent further validated the mechanism that weaker hydrogen bonds facilitated the formation of stronger covalent bonds between DES and lignin, thereby achieving the selective depolymer- ization of structural units. 3.6. Repeatability of DES in PS'S pretreatment A key advantage of using DES for lignocellulosic fractionation is the recyclability of solvents, which determines its feasibility as a reaction solvent in biorefineries [59]. This work evaluated the recyclability of CBL (CTAB:LA) with the best pretreatment performance under optimal conditions (1:6, 120 °C). The results indicated that the changes in xylan and lignin content of PS progressively diminished as the number of CBL reuse cycles increased. As depicted in Fig. 9a, the recycled CBL exhibited consistently lower lignin and xylan removal efficiencies when applied to PS compared to fresh CBL pretreatment. After five cycles, the xylan removal decreased from 90.5 % to 50.8 %, while lignin removal dropped from 64.8 % to 33.8 %. Notably, the rate of decline was more pronounced in the last two cycles than in the first three. Fig. 9b showed that SD_LX also reflected this phenomenon, initially decreasing gradually from 3.3 to 2.5, and subsequently dropping sharply to 1.3. Concurrently, the varying removal efficiency of CBL pretreatment resulted in a progressive decline in the cellulose digestibility of PS from 76.2 % to 44.5 %. Lots of studies have demonstrated that the thermostability of recovered DES and its doped degradation products, which were derived from ligno-cellulose such as phenols, organic acids, or aldehydes, significantly affected their repeatability [16,51]. Xie et al. reported that the extraction efficiency of lignin from pine using benzyltrimethyl ammonium chloride:formic acid pretreatment decreased from 78 % to 67 % after five cycles [60]. It was also observed that the acidity of DES (ChCl:acetic acid) and thermostability of HBD were decreased by two cycles, resulting in a reduction of approximately 23 % in the enzymatic digestibility of sugarcane bagasse when it was reused for pretreatment [42]. Although the efficiency of CBL pretreatment declined by approximately 42 % following five consecutive cycles (the first two cycles only decreased by 19 %), it continued to demonstrate markedly superior performance and sustainability in comparison to conventional chemical pretreatment methods. Therefore, despite a moderate decrease in the reusability of DES, its considerable promise for large-scale industrial applications in biorefining remains firmly intact. In this work, the DES incorporating CTAB as HBA was selected to achieve effective fractionation and saccharification of PS, representing a notable innovation.

4. Conclusion This work elucidated the advantages of diverse alkylammonium halide-based DES pretreatment in heightening cellulose digestibility of PS. The results demonstrated that the DES with CTAB as HBA possessed higher polarity, superior thermostability, and lower hydrogen bond energy compared to short-chain DTAB or chlorinated CTAC-based DES. The distinctive attributes of CBL ultimately resulted in the successful fractionation of 68.4 % lignin and 94.0 % xylan from PS, achieving a cellulose digestibility of 76.5 %. Characterization results indicated that the PS pretreated with CBL exhibited high accessibility and CrI, aligned with a reduced surface area of lignin. These findings underscored the effective disruption of the recalcitrant structure in PS by CBL. Quantum chemical calculations and NMR analysis revealed that the CBL disrupted the aromatic structure of lignin to a significantly greater extent compared to other DES, thereby demonstrating its exceptionally high efficacy. The proposal of innovative CBL broadened the category of DES and contributed to the sustainable and green advancement of biorefinery.

This work constructed a series of DES systems by employing diverse alkylammonium halide as HBAs, enabling an investigation into the synergistic interplay between alkyl chain length and halide anion identity on the deconstruction of poplar sawdust (PS). Notably, the cetyl-trimethylammonium bromide (CTAB)-based DES displayed a reduced surface potential, weakened hydrogen bonding energy, and diminished polarity, outperforming counterparts based on short-chain alkylamines or alternative halide-containing HBA. When applied in the pretreatment of PS, this DES has achieved a removal of 68.4% lignin and 94.0% xylan, while elevating the cellulose digestibility to 76.5%. Structural analysis unveiled that the CTAB-based DES profoundly disrupted the pivotal β-O-4 ether bonds and aromatic structure within lignin, and thus enhancing substrate digestibility. The long-chain hydrophobic alkyl chains and highly-polar bromide ions empowered the DES with superior penetration and deconstruction capabilities toward lignocellulose, highlighting the paramount significance of HBA's molecular structure in refining DES pretreatment paradigms for efficient biomass transformation. # 1. Introduction The overreliance on fossil resources and the challenges posed by global climate change necessitates the emergence of renewable re- sources as a solution to the energy crisis [1]. The bioconversion of abundant and renewable lignocellulosic biomass into green bioenergy is anticipated to facilitate the sustainable development of industrialization [2,3]. Populus euramericana, a species extensively cultivated across temperate and cold-temperate zones of the Northern Hemisphere, is prized for its remarkable adaptability and pivotal role in industrial timber production [4]. However, during the processes of harvesting and manufacturing, approximately 30 % of the resulting byproduct mani- fests as fine particulate matter, commonly known as poplar sawdust (PS) [5]. Much like other lignocellulosic biomass, PS predominantly consists of glucan and xylan, which constitute the fundamental framework of its carbohydrate-rich structure [6]. As such, transforming PS into bioenergy not only presents a promising economic opportunity but also embodies a sustainable and ecologically responsible strategy for waste valorization. It is widely recognized that lignin, which envelops bioglycans such as cellulose and hemicellulose, forms a complex barrier structure that significantly impedes the biotransformation of lignocellulose [7]. To achieve efficient conversion of wood-based lignocellulose, selecting appropriate delignification pretreatment methods is crucial [8]. Nevertheless, traditional delignification pretreatments always have inherent drawbacks that have limited the development of biorefineries [9]. For instance, the oxidative methods frequently resulted in severe cellulose degradation through over-oxidation [1]. Alkaline processes gave rise to copious amounts of saline effluent [10]. Organic solvent- based systems incurred prohibitively high operational expenses, while ionic liquid treatments were plagued by excessive viscosity and inade- quate process efficiency [11]. The hydrogen bonds between HBA and HBD are the predominant internal non-covalent interactions, playing a crucial role in disrupting the lignocellulosic barrier structure [13]. During the DES pretreatment, the most widely recognized delignifica- tion mechanism involved the protons generated from the dissociation of HBD catalyzing the cleavage of ether or ester bonds between lignin and polysaccharide components [14,15]. Furthermore, the HBA would also cleave the Cα site of lignin, subsequently facilitating the cleavage of the β-O-4 bond and generating Hibbert's ketones [16]. For various DES, key properties influencing lignin dissolution included viscosity, pKa, hydrogen bond basicity, and Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters, all closely related to HBA characteristics [17]. Therefore, while numerous studies have concentrated on the relationship between HBD of DES and pretreatment performance, it was undeniable that HBAs also played a crucial role in determining the solubility of lignin in DES [15]. According to the existing literature, DES prepared using HBD pri- marily comprised organic acids and polyols, whereas HBA predomi- nantly consisted of choline chloride (ChCl) and betaine [14,18]. Regarding pretreatment performance, organic acid-based DES enriched with -COOH and -OH groups exhibited strong correlations with delignification efficiency [19,20]. This was attributed to these organic acids significantly enhancing hemicellulose removal by catalyzing the disintegration of glycosidic bonds and acetyl groups, thereby intensi- fying the degradation of lignin [5]. For instance, Tian et al. found that formic acid, acetic acid, and lactic acid-based DES achieved delignifi- cation extents of 73–77 % and selectivity up to 6 % when treating PS [21]. Hou et al. discovered that the strong electron-withdrawing groups and low pKa of the HBD in acid-based DES facilitated the dissolution of xylan from rice straw [22]. To achieve higher efficiency, acid-based DES can be combined with acid auxiliary agents, such as inorganic acids or metal chlorides, to form ternary DES, thereby ulteriorly improving the depolymerization of xylan and lignin [23,24]. Numerous studies have focused on enhancing the performance of acid-based DES pretreatment by optimizing the acidity or diversity of HBD, while overlooking the potential of alternative HBA beyond quaternary ammonium salts. Ling et al. treated bamboo with DES prepared from different HBA, specif- ically acetamide, betaine, and ChCl. They discovered that levulinic acid/ ChCl exhibited the strongest delignification properties, while levulinic acid/betaine demonstrated superior lignin recovery capabilities [25]. Additionally, it has been reported that a shorter-alkyl-chain in quater- nary ammonium salts within DES was more favorable for the dissolution of lignin and xylan, indicating that the selectivity of the HBA signifi- cantly influenced pretreatment performance [19]. Our previously works also found that DES prepared by alkylammonium bromide/chloride has unpredictable effects during pretreatments [26]. Specifically, the syn- ergistic effect of cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) combined with lactic acid (LA) could achieve the removal of more than 50 % of lignin and 73 % of xylan [27]. This violently disrupted the natural structure of lignocellulose, thereby validating the potential of alky- lammonium halide-based DES in biorefinery applications. As the HBA of DES, alkylammonium halides not only exhibited electron-dense domains adept at forming robust hydrogen bonds that promoted efficient eutectic formation, but also boasted extended hydrocarbon chains that conferred pronounced hydrophobicity upon the solvent matrix [28]. This inherent lipophilic character may potentially enhance the extraction efficacy of hydrophobic constituents from lignocellulose. Despite these promising attributes, previous researches have largely been limited to preliminary evaluations of DES pretreatment performance. A deeper mechanistic understanding of how critical structural parameters of HBA (such as the alkyl chain length, the halogen atom type, and the functional group architecture of alkylammonium halides) influenced the overall effi- ciency of the pretreatment process remained strikingly underexplored. Moreover, the relationship between the structural features of DES’s HBA and the deconstruction of lignin required further elucidation. The objective of this study was to investigate the competitive behavior of alkylammonium or ChCl-based DES in the separation of PS components, and to evaluate the potential applications of lower-cost and higher- biocompatibility alkylammonium halides in biorefining processes. In this study, DES were prepared by combining three types of alkylammonium salts or ChCl with LA. The structural characteristics of the prepared DES were thoroughly analyzed using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), proton nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and Quantum theoretical calculation. Subsequently, these DES were utilized for PS pretreatment, and the cellulose digestibility of the pretreated PS was evaluated. The effects of DES on PS were examined through changes in crystal structure, accessibility, lignin surface area, and lignin structural characterization. Finally, the recyclability of the DES was examined to evaluate their potential application in lignocellulosic pretreatment, and recommendations for optimizing DES pretreatment were provided. 2. Quantum theory analysis of DES and DES:VG The molecular structures of CTAB, CTAC, DTAB, ChCl and LA were optimized by Gaussian09 at M062X/6-311 + g(d,p) level [17]. The lignin model compound utilized in this study was veratrylglycerol-β-guaiacyl ether (VG), which contained β-O-4 ether linkages, aromatic hydroxyl groups, and two aliphatic hydroxyl groups. The cluster structures of various DES and their clusters formed with VG were constructed using MOPAC and Gaussian09 programs. For each cluster, 20 random cluster configurations were generated. These configurations were initially optimized semi-empirically at the PM6-DH⁺ level, followed by further refinement using Gaussian09 at the B3LYP/6-31G* level to obtain detailed molecular electrostatic potential information. The electron density (ρBCP) and the Laplace of the electron density (∇²ρBCP) were calculated for each DES and their clusters formed with VG. Ultimately, the lowest-energy configuration was selected from the 20 random configurations, and subsequent analyses were performed using the Multiwfn program, including molecular surface electrostatic potential calculations, atoms-in-molecules (AIM) analysis, and Independent Gradient Model with Hydrogen (IGMH) analysis. ## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Property difference of DES #### 3.1.1. Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters To investigate the unique properties of DES, four distinct samples composed of ChCl:LA (CCL), CTAB:LA (CBL), DTAB:LA (DBL), and CTAC:LA (CAL) were prepared with a molar ratio of HBD to HBA set at 1:4. The multiparametric K-T parameters including the hydrogen bond acidity (α), hydrogen bond basicity (β), and polarizability (π*), were utilized to quantitatively evaluate the polarity characteristics of these DES [30]. As presented in Table 1, alkylammonium-based DES have the lower π* values compared to traditional CCL, specifically 0.83 for CBL, 0.59 for DBL, and 0.31 for CAL. Given that HBD was consistently comprised of an equal amount of LA, the predominant factors influencing the polarizability of these DES were attributed to the structural characteristics of HBA [31,32]. Specifically, the O in -OH group of the ChCl molecule possessed high electronegativity, whereas the C in -CH3 group of the alkylammonium-based DES displayed relatively uniform electronegativity [33]. Additionally, due to the lower electronegativity of Br⁻ compared to Cl⁻, the positive charge distribution in the CTAB molecule was more concentrated, resulting in higher polarity [34]. Notably, the DTAB with shorter alkyl chain had higher polarity than CTAB, likely due to differences in solubility and amphiphilicity [35]. Table 1 also presented the β parameter, which quantified the ability of DES to facilitate proton association through hydrogen bonding. The values were ranked as follows: CAL (1.08) > DBL (1.02) > CCL (0.74) > CBL (0.57). The capability of HBA to form hydrogen bonds was primarily characterized by its ability to donate electron density [36]. Specifically, the N in quaternary ammonium structures of both ChCl or alkylammonium halides could provide electron density, thereby facilitating hydrogen bond formation [37,38]. Even with the identical HBD, DES displayed varying proton-supplying capacities, which were also closely related to the characteristics of HBA. Studies have shown that ChCl exhibited greater instability under acidic conditions compared to CTAB, negatively impacting its proton-providing capability associated with HBD [40]. Conversely, CTAB, with longer alkyl chain and acid instability, demonstrated adverse proton acceptance performance [41]. Moreover, CTAB was less likely to provide protons compared to CTAC due to the higher stability of Br⁻ relative to Cl⁻ [35]. In summary, the K- T parameter characteristics of DES showed a profound and intricate relationship with the structural attributes of HBA, consequently influ- encing the dissolution behavior of non-polar polymers. Quantum chemical calculation Atoms in Molecules (AIM) theory was employed to investigate the intermolecular interactions within the DES [17]. Fig. 2a illustrated the bond critical points (BCP) associated with hydrogen bonds in the four DES, while Table S1 summarized the corresponding electron density (ρBCP) and Laplace function of the electron density (∇²ρBCP). According to AIM theory, the standard range of ρBCP in hydrogen bonds was 0.002 to 0.035 a.u., and the ∇²ρBCP values generally fell between 0.024 and 0.139 a.u. [15,44]. The ρBCP and ∇²ρBCP values between HBA and HBD for all four DES were within these specified ranges, confirming that their predominant interaction mode was hydrogen bonding. Subsequently, the hydrogen bond energy (HBE) was calculated and categorized into four classes: weak (> − 2.5 kcal/mol), weak-medium (−2.5 to −14.0 kcal/mol), medium (−15.0 to −11.0 kcal/mol), and strong (<−15.0 kcal/mol) [44]. According to Table S1, the HBE between the halogen ions of CTAB, CTAC and DTAB with LA were − 7.656, −8.681 and − 9.848 kcal/mol, respectively. In contrast, the HBE between Cl in ChCl and LA was measured at −8.829 kcal/mol. These findings suggested that alkylammonium halide-based DES exhibited strong internal hydrogen bonding, with the most pronounced effect observed in short-chain brominated DTAB as HBA. Fig. 2b presented a van der Waals surface diagram illustrating the electrostatic potential coloring for various DES. Notably, there were negative electrostatic potentials near the Cl⁻ or Br⁻ of the HBA and the hydroxyl O of LA, while substantial positive potentials were observed near H and methyl groups. This confirmed that the pronounced negative potential surrounding functional group indicated their suitability as HBA, whereas the strong positive potential suggested their appropriateness as HBD [48]. The formation of hydrogen bonds between the HBD and HBA led to charge delocalization, thereby facilitating the formation of DES [49]. In the aromatic region, the proportion of S units in lignin was notably elevated following DES pretreatment. As shown in Table 4, the proportion of S and G units in LR was 50.1 % and 49.9 %, respectively. Meanwhile, the DES could supply protons to facilitate the demethoxylation of S units, converting them into G units [56]. It has mentioned that the DES prepared with short-chain DTAB or chlorinated CTAC possessed higher hydrogen bond associations than CBL, but the depolymerization of lignin during pretreatment was inferior to that observed with CBL pretreatment. Hou et al. discovered that the hydrogen bond strength in DES was inversely proportional to their pretreatment efficiency, and the DES with higher hydrogen bond energy exhibited reduced lignin depolymerization [22]. Hence, as the hydrogen bond energy of DES decreased in the following order of CAL > DBL > CCL > CBL, the depolymerization and removal efficiency of lignin progressively increased in this work. 3.5.2. Therefore, the veratrylglycerol-β-guaiacyl ether (VG) was selected as a lignin model compound for quantum chemical calculations involving four DES systems [58]. Fig. 2a and b displayed the AIM molecular graphs and van der Waals surface maps with electrostatic potential coloring for four DES:VG clusters. The lower absolute value of the electrostatic potential suggested weaker HBD-HBA interactions, which facilitated the formation of a hydrogen bond network between DES and VG. Fig. 3b illustrated the quantitative distribution of electrostatic potential for four DES:VG clusters, aligning with the van der Waals surface diagram depicting electrostatic potential filling. It was evident that CBL:VG cluster exhibited a substantial area near an electrostatic potential of zero, followed by CAL:VG and DBL:VG, while CCL:VG displayed a notably smaller charged area. Notably, the strongest interaction was observed between LA and the O of the alcohol hydroxyl group of VG, characterized by a pBCP value of 0.0510 and a bond energy of -10.6605 kcal/mol, which belonged to the covalent bond category [44]. This further suggested that CBL exhibited a more stable covalent bond structure with lignin compared to CCL, thereby accelerating the dissolution process of lignin. The formation of stronger hydrogen bonds theoretically indicated that lignin rich in β-O-4 was more easily dissolved in CBL, and the quantitative results of lignin linkage bonds well confirmed this. Repeatability of DES in PS'S pretreatment A key advantage of using DES for lignocellulosic fractionation is the recyclability of solvents, which determines its feasibility as a reaction solvent in biorefineries [59]. This work evaluated the recyclability of CBL (CTAB:LA) with the best pretreatment performance under optimal conditions (1:6, 120 °C). The results indicated that the changes in xylan and lignin content of PS progressively diminished as the number of CBL reuse cycles increased. As depicted in Fig. 9a, the recycled CBL exhibited consistently lower lignin and xylan removal efficiencies when applied to PS compared to fresh CBL pretreatment. After five cycles, the xylan removal decreased from 90.5 % to 50.8 %, while lignin removal dropped from 64.8 % to 33.8 %. Notably, the rate of decline was more pronounced in the last two cycles than in the first three. Fig. 9b showed that SD_LX also reflected this phenomenon, initially decreasing gradually from 3.3 to 2.5, and subsequently dropping sharply to 1.3. Concurrently, the varying removal efficiency of CBL pretreatment resulted in a progressive decline in the cellulose digestibility of PS from 76.2 % to 44.5 %. Lots of studies have demonstrated that the thermostability of recovered DES and its doped degradation products, which were derived from ligno-cellulose such as phenols, organic acids, or aldehydes, significantly affected their repeatability [16,51]. Xie et al. reported that the extraction efficiency of lignin from pine using benzyltrimethyl ammonium chloride:formic acid pretreatment decreased from 78 % to 67 % after five cycles [60]. It was also observed that the acidity of DES (ChCl:acetic acid) and thermostability of HBD were decreased by two cycles, resulting in a reduction of approximately 23 % in the enzymatic digestibility of sugarcane bagasse when it was reused for pretreatment [42]. Although the efficiency of CBL pretreatment declined by approximately 42 % following five consecutive cycles (the first two cycles only decreased by 19 %), it continued to demonstrate markedly superior performance and sustainability in comparison to conventional chemical pretreatment methods. Therefore, despite a moderate decrease in the reusability of DES, its considerable promise for large-scale industrial applications in biorefining remains firmly intact. In this work, the DES incorporating CTAB as HBA was selected to achieve effective fractionation and saccharification of PS, representing a notable innovation. 4. Conclusion This work elucidated the advantages of diverse alkylammonium halide-based DES pretreatment in heightening cellulose digestibility of PS. The results demonstrated that the DES with CTAB as HBA possessed higher polarity, superior thermostability, and lower hydrogen bond energy compared to short-chain DTAB or chlorinated CTAC-based DES. The distinctive attributes of CBL ultimately resulted in the successful fractionation of 68.4 % lignin and 94.0 % xylan from PS, achieving a cellulose digestibility of 76.5 %. Characterization results indicated that the PS pretreated with CBL exhibited high accessibility and CrI, aligned with a reduced surface area of lignin. These findings underscored the effective disruption of the recalcitrant structure in PS by CBL. Quantum chemical calculations and NMR analysis revealed that the CBL disrupted the aromatic structure of lignin to a significantly greater extent compared to other DES, thereby demonstrating its exceptionally high efficacy. The proposal of innovative CBL broadened the category of DES and contributed to the sustainable and green advancement of biorefinery. **Declaration of competing interest** The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. ## Acknowledgements The authors gratefully acknowledge the financial support of this work by the Youth Project of National Natural Science Foundation of China (32301531), the Basic Science (Natural science) Research Project of Higher Education Institutions in Jiangsu Province (23KJB220001), the Fourth Cultivation Project of Leader-type Innovative Talent Introduction of Changzhou 'Longcheng Talent Plan' (CQ20230084), and the Changzhou Sci&Tech Program (CJ20241085). Introduction The overreliance on fossil resources and the challenges posed by global climate change necessitates the emergence of renewable re- sources as a solution to the energy crisis [1]. The bioconversion of abundant and renewable lignocellulosic biomass into green bioenergy is anticipated to facilitate the sustainable development of industrialization [2,3]. Populus euramericana, a species extensively cultivated across temperate and cold-temperate zones of the Northern Hemisphere, is prized for its remarkable adaptability and pivotal role in industrial timber production [4]. However, during the processes of harvesting and manufacturing, approximately 30 % of the resulting byproduct mani- fests as fine particulate matter, commonly known as poplar sawdust (PS) [5]. Much like other lignocellulosic biomass, PS predominantly consists of glucan and xylan, which constitute the fundamental framework of its carbohydrate-rich structure [6]. As such, transforming PS into bioenergy not only presents a promising economic opportunity but also embodies a sustainable and ecologically responsible strategy for waste valorization. It is widely recognized that lignin, which envelops bioglycans such as cellulose and hemicellulose, forms a complex barrier structure that significantly impedes the biotransformation of lignocellulose [7]. To achieve efficient conversion of wood-based lignocellulose, selecting appropriate delignification pretreatment methods is crucial [8]. Nevertheless, traditional delignification pretreatments always have inherent drawbacks that have limited the development of biorefineries [9]. For instance, the oxidative methods frequently resulted in severe cellulose degradation through over-oxidation [1]. Alkaline processes gave rise to copious amounts of saline effluent [10]. Organic solvent- based systems incurred prohibitively high operational expenses, while ionic liquid treatments were plagued by excessive viscosity and inade- quate process efficiency [11]. The hydrogen bonds between HBA and HBD are the predominant internal non-covalent interactions, playing a crucial role in disrupting the lignocellulosic barrier structure [13]. During the DES pretreatment, the most widely recognized delignifica- tion mechanism involved the protons generated from the dissociation of HBD catalyzing the cleavage of ether or ester bonds between lignin and polysaccharide components [14,15]. Furthermore, the HBA would also cleave the Cα site of lignin, subsequently facilitating the cleavage of the β-O-4 bond and generating Hibbert's ketones [16]. For various DES, key properties influencing lignin dissolution included viscosity, pKa, hydrogen bond basicity, and Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters, all closely related to HBA characteristics [17]. Therefore, while numerous studies have concentrated on the relationship between HBD of DES and pretreatment performance, it was undeniable that HBAs also played a crucial role in determining the solubility of lignin in DES [15]. According to the existing literature, DES prepared using HBD pri- marily comprised organic acids and polyols, whereas HBA predomi- nantly consisted of choline chloride (ChCl) and betaine [14,18]. Regarding pretreatment performance, organic acid-based DES enriched with -COOH and -OH groups exhibited strong correlations with delignification efficiency [19,20]. This was attributed to these organic acids significantly enhancing hemicellulose removal by catalyzing the disintegration of glycosidic bonds and acetyl groups, thereby intensi- fying the degradation of lignin [5]. For instance, Tian et al. found that formic acid, acetic acid, and lactic acid-based DES achieved delignifi- cation extents of 73–77 % and selectivity up to 6 % when treating PS [21]. Hou et al. discovered that the strong electron-withdrawing groups and low pKa of the HBD in acid-based DES facilitated the dissolution of xylan from rice straw [22]. To achieve higher efficiency, acid-based DES can be combined with acid auxiliary agents, such as inorganic acids or metal chlorides, to form ternary DES, thereby ulteriorly improving the depolymerization of xylan and lignin [23,24]. Numerous studies have focused on enhancing the performance of acid-based DES pretreatment by optimizing the acidity or diversity of HBD, while overlooking the potential of alternative HBA beyond quaternary ammonium salts. Ling et al. treated bamboo with DES prepared from different HBA, specif- ically acetamide, betaine, and ChCl. They discovered that levulinic acid/ ChCl exhibited the strongest delignification properties, while levulinic acid/betaine demonstrated superior lignin recovery capabilities [25]. Additionally, it has been reported that a shorter-alkyl-chain in quater- nary ammonium salts within DES was more favorable for the dissolution of lignin and xylan, indicating that the selectivity of the HBA signifi- cantly influenced pretreatment performance [19]. Our previously works also found that DES prepared by alkylammonium bromide/chloride has unpredictable effects during pretreatments [26]. Specifically, the syn- ergistic effect of cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) combined with lactic acid (LA) could achieve the removal of more than 50 % of lignin and 73 % of xylan [27]. This violently disrupted the natural structure of lignocellulose, thereby validating the potential of alky- lammonium halide-based DES in biorefinery applications. As the HBA of DES, alkylammonium halides not only exhibited electron-dense domains adept at forming robust hydrogen bonds that promoted efficient eutectic formation, but also boasted extended hydrocarbon chains that conferred pronounced hydrophobicity upon the solvent matrix [28]. This inherent lipophilic character may potentially enhance the extraction efficacy of hydrophobic constituents from lignocellulose. Despite these promising attributes, previous researches have largely been limited to preliminary evaluations of DES pretreatment performance. A deeper mechanistic understanding of how critical structural parameters of HBA (such as the alkyl chain length, the halogen atom type, and the functional group architecture of alkylammonium halides) influenced the overall effi- ciency of the pretreatment process remained strikingly underexplored. Moreover, the relationship between the structural features of DES’s HBA and the deconstruction of lignin required further elucidation. The effects of DES on PS were examined through changes in crystal structure, accessibility, lignin surface area, and lignin structural characterization. Repeatability of DES in PS'S pretreatment A key advantage of using DES for lignocellulosic fractionation is the recyclability of solvents, which determines its feasibility as a reaction solvent in biorefineries [59]. This work evaluated the recyclability of CBL (CTAB:LA) with the best pretreatment performance under optimal conditions (1:6, 120 °C). The results indicated that the changes in xylan and lignin content of PS progressively diminished as the number of CBL reuse cycles increased. As depicted in Fig. 9a, the recycled CBL exhibited consistently lower lignin and xylan removal efficiencies when applied to PS compared to fresh CBL pretreatment. After five cycles, the xylan removal decreased from 90.5 % to 50.8 %, while lignin removal dropped from 64.8 % to 33.8 %. Notably, the rate of decline was more pronounced in the last two cycles than in the first three. Fig. 9b showed that SD_LX also reflected this phenomenon, initially decreasing gradually from 3.3 to 2.5, and subsequently dropping sharply to 1.3. Concurrently, the varying removal efficiency of CBL pretreatment resulted in a progressive decline in the cellulose digestibility of PS from 76.2 % to 44.5 %. Lots of studies have demonstrated that the thermostability of recovered DES and its doped degradation products, which were derived from ligno-cellulose such as phenols, organic acids, or aldehydes, significantly affected their repeatability [16,51]. Xie et al. reported that the extraction efficiency of lignin from pine using benzyltrimethyl ammonium chloride:formic acid pretreatment decreased from 78 % to 67 % after five cycles [60]. It was also observed that the acidity of DES (ChCl:acetic acid) and thermostability of HBD were decreased by two cycles, resulting in a reduction of approximately 23 % in the enzymatic digestibility of sugarcane bagasse when it was reused for pretreatment [42]. Although the efficiency of CBL pretreatment declined by approximately 42 % following five consecutive cycles (the first two cycles only decreased by 19 %), it continued to demonstrate markedly superior performance and sustainability in comparison to conventional chemical pretreatment methods. Therefore, despite a moderate decrease in the reusability of DES, its considerable promise for large-scale industrial applications in biorefining remains firmly intact. In this work, the DES incorporating CTAB as HBA was selected to achieve effective fractionation and saccharification of PS, representing a notable innovation. 4. Conclusion This work elucidated the advantages of diverse alkylammonium halide-based DES pretreatment in heightening cellulose digestibility of PS. The results demonstrated that the DES with CTAB as HBA possessed higher polarity, superior thermostability, and lower hydrogen bond energy compared to short-chain DTAB or chlorinated CTAC-based DES. The distinctive attributes of CBL ultimately resulted in the successful fractionation of 68.4 % lignin and 94.0 % xylan from PS, achieving a cellulose digestibility of 76.5 %. Characterization results indicated that the PS pretreated with CBL exhibited high accessibility and CrI, aligned with a reduced surface area of lignin. These findings underscored the effective disruption of the recalcitrant structure in PS by CBL. Quantum chemical calculations and NMR analysis revealed that the CBL disrupted the aromatic structure of lignin to a significantly greater extent compared to other DES, thereby demonstrating its exceptionally high efficacy. The proposal of innovative CBL broadened the category of DES and contributed to the sustainable and green advancement of biorefinery. **Declaration of competing interest** The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. ## Acknowledgements The authors gratefully acknowledge the financial support of this work by the Youth Project of National Natural Science Foundation of China (32301531), the Basic Science (Natural science) Research Project of Higher Education Institutions in Jiangsu Province (23KJB220001), the Fourth Cultivation Project of Leader-type Innovative Talent Introduction of Changzhou 'Longcheng Talent Plan' (CQ20230084), and the Changzhou Sci&Tech Program (CJ20241085).
